papers.title: Roles of autophagy in brain homeostasis and disease.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how autophagy, the cell's process for degrading and recycling damaged components, contributes to maintaining normal brain function. It likely discusses how disruptions in autophagy pathways are linked to neurodegenerative and other brain diseases. As a review, it probably synthesizes current understanding of autophagy's mechanisms and regulation specifically in neural tissue.
papers.why: This review likely provides foundational context on autophagy's role in neuronal health and disease, directly supporting the mechanistic framework needed for the PhD project's focus on mitophagy in neurons.

papers.title: Remimazolam Attenuates Neurological Injury After TBI: A Potential Role of α7nAChR-Associated Mitophagy Enhancement and Pyroptosis Suppression in BV2 Cells.
papers.summary: This study examines whether Remimazolam, a sedative drug, can reduce brain injury after traumatic brain injury (TBI) using BV2 microglial cells as a model. The researchers found that Remimazolam appears to work by activating a receptor called α7nAChR, which boosts mitophagy (a process that clears damaged mitochondria) while suppressing pyroptosis (a form of inflammatory cell death). These findings suggest a potential therapeutic mechanism where enhancing mitochondrial quality control reduces harmful inflammation in microglia after brain trauma.
papers.why: While focused on microglia rather than neurons, this paper's mechanistic insights into mitophagy regulation via α7nAChR signaling could inform interpretation of mitophagy-related spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic signatures in neuroinflammatory contexts relevant to the broader brain injury and autophagy literature.

papers.title: No Large Absolute Shift in the Mitochondrial Chaperonin–Import Axis in Autism Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex
papers.summary: This study looked at whether key mitochondrial proteins involved in chaperone function and protein import are significantly altered in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of people with autism. The researchers found no large or consistent absolute changes in this mitochondrial chaperonin-import pathway when comparing autism brain tissue to controls. This suggests that, at least in this brain region and pathway, mitochondrial import machinery is not a major driver of autism-related pathology.
papers.why: While focused on autism rather than interneurons or perineuronal nets, this paper's methodology for probing mitochondrial protein import and chaperone pathways in cortical tissue is directly relevant to mitophagy research in neurons and could inform how spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic data on mitochondrial health are interpreted in other neuropsychiatric or neurodevelopmental contexts.
papers.figure: A figure showing quantified protein levels (e.g., western blot or immunohistochemistry) of chaperonin and import machinery components across autism vs. control DLPFC samples.

papers.title: JP1 peptide modulates oxidative stress and autophagy via Keap1-Nrf2-ARE in ALS model mice.
papers.summary: This study tests a peptide called JP1 in a mouse model of ALS, a neurodegenerative disease that damages motor neurons. JP1 appears to work by activating the Keap1-Nrf2-ARE pathway, which is a major cellular defense system against oxidative stress. The researchers found that JP1 also influences autophagy, the process cells use to clear damaged components, suggesting it could help protect neurons in ALS.
papers.why: This paper connects oxidative stress, the Keap1-Nrf2-ARE pathway, and autophagy regulation in neurons, offering mechanistic insight relevant to mitophagy/autophagy research even though it focuses on ALS rather than interneurons or spatial omics directly.
papers.figure: Figure showing autophagy marker (e.g., LC3-II/p62) and Nrf2 pathway protein levels in spinal cord/motor neuron tissue of JP1-treated vs untreated ALS mice.

papers.title: Therapeutic potential and underlying mechanisms of engineered young plasma-derived exosomes in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.summary: This paper investigates whether exosomes engineered from young plasma can help treat Alzheimer's disease. Exosomes are tiny cell-derived vesicles that carry proteins and genetic material, and 'young' plasma is thought to contain more youthful, potentially rejuvenating signals compared to aged plasma. The study likely explores how these engineered exosomes affect disease-related processes in the brain, such as protein clearance or neuronal health, in an Alzheimer's model.
papers.why: While focused on Alzheimer's therapeutics rather than mitophagy or interneurons directly, exosome-mediated mechanisms often involve autophagy and protein clearance pathways relevant to neurodegenerative processes in your project's broader scope.

papers.title: Mitochondrial-neuroimmune interfaces in post-stroke spasticity: from acute brain injury to chronic motor phenotypes.
papers.summary: This paper is a conceptual review-style article proposing that mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroimmune signaling interact to drive spasticity (abnormal muscle tightness) after stroke. It suggests that damage occurring in the acute phase of brain injury sets off mitochondrial and immune changes that persist and contribute to chronic motor problems. The abstract does not provide specific experimental data, methods, or figures, indicating this is likely a hypothesis or narrative review paper.
papers.why: Although focused on stroke and motor spasticity rather than neurons' spatial biology, it touches on mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroimmune interactions in the brain, which are tangential to the mitophagy focus of the profile but lack direct relevance to interneurons, perineuronal nets, or spatial omics/AI methods.

papers.title: Presequences of non-imported mitochondrial proteins serve as quality control elements in the cytosol
papers.summary: This paper investigates what happens to mitochondrial proteins that carry N-terminal targeting sequences (presequences) but fail to be imported into mitochondria. The researchers find that these presequences act as quality control tags, marking the non-imported proteins for recognition and clearance by cytosolic protein quality control machinery. This reveals a new layer of proteostasis regulation that protects the cytosol from accumulation of mistargeted mitochondrial precursor proteins.
papers.why: Since mitophagy relies on proper detection of dysfunctional mitochondrial components, understanding how cytosolic quality control of non-imported mitochondrial precursor proteins operates could inform how proteostasis and organelle stress intersect with mitophagy pathways in neurons.
